## Why analog, and why first {#sec-filt-why}

Aliasing folds energy above the Nyquist frequency $f_s/2$ down into the band
that is actually sampled [@oppenheim]. Once that folding has happened, no
later processing — digital filtering, windowing, anything done to the
samples after the fact — can separate the folded component from a real
component that already sits at the same frequency: the information about
where it came from was destroyed at the instant of sampling. The only place
to remove that energy is before the sample is taken, in the analog domain.
That is what this stage does, and it is why it sits ahead of the ADC — after
the [conditioning board's](conditioning-board.qmd) gain, so it filters a
signal already scaled into a useful range, but with nothing digital between
it and the converter. [S3](../experiments/S3-aliasing-filtering/index.qmd)
measures folding directly, predicted against observed; this page designs the
stage that experiment characterizes.

## First-order RC {#sec-filt-rc1}

A single-pole low-pass, $H(s) = 1/(1+sRC)$, has corner frequency

$$
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}
$$ {#eq-filt-fc}

with magnitude and phase, at real frequency $f$,

$$
|H(f)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}},
\qquad
\phi(f) = -\arctan\!\left(\frac{f}{f_c}\right)
$$ {#eq-filt-mag-phase}

Group delay — the delay a filter imposes on the envelope of a narrowband
signal, and the quantity that matters for how a filter smears a *transient*
rather than a sinusoid — follows from the phase:

$$
\tau_g(f) = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\phi}{df} = \frac{RC}{1+(2\pi f RC)^2}
$$ {#eq-filt-groupdelay}

As $f\to 0$, $\tau_g \to RC = 1/(2\pi f_c)$: a filter with a low corner
delays and rounds a fast transient by an amount comparable to its own time
constant. This is exactly the effect [T2's plunge
test](../experiments/T2-temperature-dynamic/index.qmd) has to separate from
the sensor's own thermal time constant — a filter placed ahead of a
step-response measurement adds its own first-order lag in series with the
one being measured, and if the two time constants are not clearly separated,
the fitted $\tau$ belongs to neither the sensor nor the filter alone.

## Higher order {#sec-filt-order}

A single RC section rolls off at $-20\,$dB/decade for $f \gg f_c$. Two ways
to increase that slope: cascade more passive sections, or build an active
multi-pole stage.

**Cascading passive sections does not simply multiply the rolloff at the
original corner.** If $N$ identical, buffered (non-interacting) first-order
sections are cascaded, the combined magnitude is $|H(f)|^N$, and at $f=f_c$
each section already contributes $1/\sqrt2$, so the cascade's own $-3\,$dB
point is not $f_c$ but

$$
f_{c,N} = f_c\sqrt{2^{1/N}-1}
$$ {#eq-filt-cascade-fc}

which is *below* $f_c$: two sections at "the same $f_c$" reach $-3\,$dB at
about $0.64\,f_c$, not at $f_c$. The asymptotic $-20N\,$dB/decade slope is
only approached well above $f_c$. And if the sections are not buffered from
each other, the second stage loads the first, so the transfer function is
not even the product $|H(f)|^N$ — the poles shift from what the individual
$R$s and $C$s alone would suggest, and the effective corner and rolloff have
to be recomputed as one higher-order network, not assembled from independent
one-stage numbers.

**An active stage** — a Sallen–Key topology, one op-amp and four passive
components implementing a full two-pole section — avoids the interaction
problem by construction, since the op-amp's low output impedance decouples
what would otherwise load the network, and gives control over the pole
placement through a single parameter, the quality factor $Q$, in the
standard second-order form

$$
H(s) = \frac{\omega_0^2}{s^2 + \dfrac{\omega_0}{Q}s + \omega_0^2},
\qquad
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{R_1R_2C_1C_2}},
\qquad
Q = \frac{\sqrt{R_1R_2C_1/C_2}}{R_1+R_2}
$$ {#eq-filt-sk}

for the unity-gain Sallen–Key low-pass built from $R_1, R_2, C_1, C_2$
[@kester2005]. Unlike two cascaded passive sections, a single Sallen–Key
stage reaches a genuine two-pole, $-40\,$dB/decade asymptotic slope with
only one op-amp, and $Q$ can be set through the ratio of the four components
to trade a maximally-flat passband (Butterworth, $Q=1/\sqrt2$) against a
sharper knee with some peaking.

## The design problem {#sec-filt-design}

Given a sampling rate $f_s$ and a passband of interest up to
$f_\max < f_s/2$, the first folding frequency is
$f_\mathrm{fold} = f_s - f_\max$ — content at $f_\mathrm{fold}$ aliases down
to $f_\max$ once sampled. Two requirements constrain the corner frequency
$f_c$ of an $N$-th order stage with asymptotic slope $-20N\,$dB/decade:

**Stopband.** The attenuation at $f_\mathrm{fold}$ must be at least $A$ dB:

$$
f_c \;\le\; f_\mathrm{fold}\cdot 10^{-A/(20N)}
$$ {#eq-filt-stopband}

**Passband droop.** The attenuation at $f_\max$ itself must not exceed some
allowed droop $\delta$ dB:

$$
f_c \;\ge\; \frac{f_\max}{\sqrt{10^{\delta/10}-1}}
$$ {#eq-filt-passband}

@eq-filt-stopband pushes $f_c$ down; @eq-filt-passband pushes it up. A
feasible design needs the two bounds to leave a non-empty interval for
$f_c$, which is the real content of the trade-off: for fixed $A$ and
$\delta$, a higher order $N$ relaxes @eq-filt-stopband — moves its bound
upward — without touching @eq-filt-passband at all, since that bound depends
only on $f_\max$ and the droop tolerated, never on $N$. That is why a
tighter stopband requirement is answered with more poles rather than with a
lower corner: a lower corner alone would also cost passband flatness that
@eq-filt-passband is protecting.

## Component selection {#sec-filt-parts}

- **Capacitor dielectric.** Class-2 ceramics (X7R, Y5V and similar) have a
  capacitance that depends strongly on temperature — typically several
  hundred to over a thousand ppm/°C, and non-linear — and on applied DC bias,
  where a Y5V part can lose a large fraction of its nominal capacitance at
  its rated voltage. Since $f_c$ in @eq-filt-fc depends directly on $C$, a
  filter built from class-2 parts has a corner that moves with the operating
  point, not just with tolerance. Class-1 ceramics (C0G/NP0) and film
  capacitors (polyester, polypropylene) have temperature and voltage
  coefficients small enough to ignore at this level; prefer them for any $C$
  whose value sets a corner frequency, a gain, or a timing.
- **Resistor type.** Metal-film, not carbon-composition: lower tolerance and
  roughly an order of magnitude lower temperature coefficient, for the same
  reason argued for the divider's resistors on the [conditioning
  board](conditioning-board.qmd#sec-cond-dividers).

Specific values and part numbers: [TODO (Paolo)]{.todo}, once
@eq-filt-stopband and @eq-filt-passband are solved for this bench's actual
$f_s$ and $f_\max$.

## This stage in an uncertainty budget {#sec-filt-budget}

A filter with a nonzero corner relative to $f_\max$ attenuates the passband
itself, per @eq-filt-mag-phase, by a known factor $|H(f_\max)|$ at the
frequency of interest. That is a systematic effect, and once characterized —
by measuring $|H(f)|$ against a known input, the way
[S2](../experiments/S2-daq-dynamic/index.qmd) characterizes the board itself
— it becomes a *correction*, not an error: divide the reading by
$|H(f_\max)|$. What is left in the budget afterward is the uncertainty of
that correction, driven by the tolerance and drift of $R$ and $C$ entering
$f_c$, and it is carried the same way as the gain term of [the conditioning
board](conditioning-board.qmd#sec-cond-budget): multiplicative, with
sensitivity proportional to the reading.
